title_en: Nameless Heroes: The Memoirs of a Nationalist Secret Agent
description: The memoirs of Chen Gongshu, a senior operative of the Chinese Nationalist secret service (the Juntong), spanning his work from the founding of the Beiping station in 1932, through the failed 1939 attempt on Wang Jingwei at Hanoi and the Shanghai underground war against Japan, to the Nationalist–Communist fighting around Beiping and Tianjin in 1946–49. It collects the four books of his “Nameless Heroes” series.
rights: English translation prepared for private study. Original text © the estate of Chen Gongshu.
source_ref: Translated from 陈恭澍《英雄无名》 (Chen Gongshu, Nameless Heroes), 传记文学出版社 (Biographical Literature Press), Taipei; the four constituent books appeared separately in the early-to-mid 1980s.
_source_note: Source is a digital EPUB (no OCR): the collected 'Nameless Heroes' (英雄无名) tetralogy by Chen Gongshu, a Nationalist (Juntong) secret-service memoir. 45 spine documents; 43 are modeled as chapters. EXCLUDED: Text/cover.xhtml (0 chars) -> reused as the cover image; Text/nav.xhtml -> the source's own EPUB TOC, superseded by the builder's generated navigation. The source carries NO footnotes/endnotes of its own (grep for [n] in data/src: none present), so there is no source_notes stream. Every content file opens with the running-header line '英雄无名-陈恭澍'; it is furniture, not text, and is dropped at translation time. Chapter numbering is faithful to the source, INCLUDING its gaps: Part Three skips chapter 7 and splits chapter 10 into (上)/(下).
_translator_note: Rendered verbatim as the Translator's Note back-matter page.
translator_note: This is an English translation of 英雄无名 (Nameless Heroes) by Chen Gongshu (陈恭澍), made from the digital source EPUB. The book is a memoir of the Chinese Nationalist secret service — the organization Chen calls the Juntong — told from the inside by a man who ran its Beiping station, took part in the 1939 attempt on Wang Jingwei at Hanoi, directed operations in occupied Shanghai, and commanded a special unit in the Nationalist–Communist fighting around Beiping and Tianjin.

The volume collects four separately published books: Rooting Out Traitors in the North, Disgrace at Hanoi (published under the title The Full Story of the Wang Case at Hanoi), Renown Won in a Hundred Battles (the Shanghai operations), and Pacification of the Beiping–Tianjin Region. Chen wrote them in the early-to-mid 1980s; his own prefaces and the introductions collected at the front are translated here alongside the narrative.

Chen writes as an interested witness: a participant defending his own conduct and that of his service, in the political idiom of the Nationalist side (the Communist forces are “bandits,” the war of 1946–49 a “pacification”). That idiom is preserved, not softened; where a claim is contested by scholarship, the footnote says so and the text stands as written. Footnotes supply the historical, geographic, and institutional background a reader without a background in modern Chinese history would need.
Where the source is genuinely ambiguous, corrupt, or self-contradictory, the note says so rather than smoothing it over.
